_comment: kore write policy — read by koreops.py, which is the only door the web server
may use for start/stop/send/keys/input/resize. This FILE decides what is allowed;
the code does not. Editing it is a config change, not a code change: no restart.
(The file keeps its historical name `dispatch-allowlist.json`; koreops.py reads the
`kore` object below. Point koreops elsewhere with $RSI_DISPATCH_ALLOWLIST if you move it.)
nodes ['*'] means 'any node the engine can route to': the server's own host, plus
any client with a fresh entry in the agent registry (agents.json). The structural
bound there is the AGENT TOKEN a reachable client agent must honor — a shared secret,
so leaks matter. Restrict to specific IPs by listing them instead of '*'.
deny_nodes: IPs that may never be driven from here even if they are live/registered.
protected_sessions is a safety interlock, not a permission: any name listed here is
refused for ALL write verbs (start/stop/send/keys/input/resize) while reads keep
working. The mechanism lives in koreops.py `_validate()`; this list only decides WHO
it applies to. Empty by default — add a session name to make it read-only.
cwd_roots: a new session's working directory must sit under one of these prefixes.
allowed_keys: the named keys `kore_keys` may send (free-text goes through send/input).
fs: file-browser WRITES. enabled + per-op switches gate mkdir/rename/delete/put; the
node's fixed script re-checks roots+deny on every op, so this is the on/off, not the
boundary. put_chunk_bytes is NOT a size cap (uploads are unlimited, sent as many put
chunks) — it is the per-chunk raw-byte budget that keeps the whole `sh -c` command
under MAX_ARG_STRLEN (128KiB per execve arg). Delete is a HARD rm (no trash).
